steps.body: A wide rectangle can be **broken apart** into two friendlier ones. A 6-by-7 is hard? Slice the 7 into 5 + 2: now it's a 6-by-5 next to a 6-by-2. Find each area, add them — same total, easier math. Breaking apart never changes the covering.

widget.prompt: A 6-by-7 rectangle is split into a 6-by-5 and a 6-by-2. Build the sum of their areas.

commonBuilds.feedback: The two pieces get ADDED, not multiplied — 6×5 = 30 and 6×2 = 12 are separate carpets you lay side by side: 30 + 12.

widget.missFeedback: Find each piece's area (6×5 = 30, 6×2 = 12), then ADD them.
widget.successFeedback: 30 + 12 = 42 square units — and 6 × 7 = 42 too. Breaking apart kept the total.

predict.prompt: Splitting the 7 into 5 and 2 — does 6×5 plus 6×2 still cover the whole 6-by-7 rectangle?

options.label: No — some squares get counted twice

predict.reveal: The cut shares out the columns — five to one piece, two to the other — and every square lands in exactly one piece. Break-apart multiplication is just careful bookkeeping.

explanationVariants: The two pieces are 6×5 = 30 and 6×2 = 12; together 30 + 12 = 42 square units.
Same as the whole: 6 × 7 = 42. Splitting the 7 didn't change the covering.

widget.prompt: A 6-by-5 rectangle (area 30) sits beside a 6-by-2 rectangle (area 12), forming one 6-by-7. What is the total area?

commonErrors.feedback: 360 multiplied the two pieces (30 × 12) — but they're laid SIDE BY SIDE, so their areas add: 30 + 12 = 42.
30 is just the first piece. The 6-by-2 piece adds 12 more: 30 + 12 = 42.

steps.body: This is a hidden superpower: **6 × 7 = 6 × 5 + 6 × 2.** Splitting one side and handing the other side to each piece is the same trick you use to break apart hard multiplication facts. The rectangle SHOWS why it works — the squares are just regrouped, never lost.

explanationVariants: Split 8 into 5 + 3: a 7-by-5 (35) plus a 7-by-3 (21) makes 35 + 21 = 56 — same as 7 × 8.
7 × 8 = 7 × 5 + 7 × 3 = 35 + 21 = 56. The 7 rides along to both pieces.

widget.prompt: Break a 7-by-8 rectangle into a 7-by-5 and a 7-by-3. What is the total area?

commonErrors.feedback: 15 added just the split parts (5 + 3 + 7?) — build each piece first: 7×5 = 35 and 7×3 = 21, then 35 + 21.
42 is 7 × 6 — but the rectangle is 7 by 8. Split the 8 as 5 + 3: 35 + 21 = 56.

widget.fallbackFeedback: 7×5 = 35, 7×3 = 21, then add: the 7 goes with both pieces.

widget.prompt: To find the area of a 5-by-9 rectangle, sort each break-apart plan: does it give the right total?

items.feedback: Split the 9 into 5+4, the 5 rides along: 25 + 20 = 45. Same as 5×9.
5 + 3 = 8, not 9 — this split loses a whole column. The pieces must rebuild the full side.
You can split the OTHER side too: 2+3 = 5, so 18 + 27 = 45. Also honest.

widget.missFeedback: A split is honest only if the two pieces rebuild the full side (their split numbers must add back to it).
widget.successFeedback: Splits that rebuild the side (5+4, 6+3, 2+3 on the other side) all give 45; 5+3 loses a column.

explanationVariants: Slicing a rectangle just regroups its squares into two piles — none are added or lost, so the areas must add back to the whole.
The cut is only a line on paper; every unit square is still there, now counted in one piece or the other.

widget.prompt: Why does breaking a rectangle into two pieces keep the same total area?

options.label: The cut only regroups the squares — none are added or lost
options.feedback: A slice is just a line; every square still gets counted, in one piece or the other.

options.label: It doesn't — cutting makes the area smaller
options.feedback: Cutting removes no squares — they're all still there, just sorted into two groups that add back.

options.label: Because you multiply the two pieces together
options.feedback: Side-by-side pieces ADD, not multiply. And their sum equals the original because no squares moved out.

options.label: It only works for even numbers
options.feedback: Any split works — 7 as 5+2, 9 as 6+3, anything — as long as the pieces rebuild the full side.

hints: Split the 8 into friendlier numbers, like 5 + 3.
explanationVariants: Split 8 as 5 + 3: 9×5 = 45 and 9×3 = 27, so 45 + 27 = 72 — the area of the 9-by-8.
9 × 8 = 9×5 + 9×3 = 45 + 27 = 72. The break-apart turned a hard fact into two easy ones.

widget.prompt: Find the area of a 9-by-8 rectangle by breaking the 8 into 5 + 3. What is the total?

commonErrors.feedback: 63 is 9 × 7 — a split of 5 + 2, not 5 + 3. Using 5 + 3: 45 + 27 = 72.
17 added 9 + 8. Area multiplies each piece first: 9×5 = 45 and 9×3 = 27, then 45 + 27 = 72.

takeaways: Break one side into two; each piece keeps the other side; add the areas.
6 × 7 = 6×5 + 6×2 — the rectangle shows why multiplication breaks apart.
A split is honest only if the pieces rebuild the full side.
steps.teaser: next: shapes that aren't rectangles — cut them into ones that are.

concept.body: Quick rewind. Breaking apart is like **splitting a chocolate bar into two chunks** — the total chocolate stays the same, you just count it in two piles. Slice a rectangle, find each piece's area, add. Nothing is lost in the cut.

widget.prompt: A 4-by-3 (area 12) sits beside a 4-by-2 (area 8). Total area?

options.feedback: 12 + 8 = 20 — the pieces add up to the 4-by-5 whole.
96 multiplied the pieces (12 × 8). Side-by-side areas ADD: 12 + 8 = 20.
12 is just the first piece — add the second (8) for 20.
